section.title: The Two Witnesses and the Seventh Trumpet
section.sectionRationale: This chapter completes the interlude begun in chapter 10 and closes out the whole trumpet cycle. John measures the temple and its worshipers while the outer courtyard is given to trampling nations, then two empowered witnesses prophesy in sackcloth, are killed by the beast from the Abyss, and are publicly vindicated. The chapter ends with the seventh trumpet, at which loud voices in heaven declare that the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of the Lord and His Christ, the true climax the sixth trumpet's woes were building toward.
section.thesis: God measures and protects His true worshipers even while the nations trample the outer court, and His two witnesses, empowered to prophesy at great cost, are killed and gloated over but then publicly raised and taken up, a preview of the moment the seventh trumpet announces: the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ.
section.frameNote: Five beats: measuring the temple and surrendering the courtyard to the nations; the two witnesses empowered to prophesy for 1,260 days; their death and public disgrace at the hands of the beast from the Abyss; their resurrection, ascension, and the earthquake that follows; and the seventh trumpet, announcing that the kingdom has come and the time for judgment and reward has arrived.

units.label: Measuring the temple
units.note: the worshipers counted, the courtyard given over

verses.text: Then I was given a measuring rod like a staff and was told, "Go and measure the {{naos|temple}} of God and the altar, and count the number of worshipers there.
But exclude the courtyard outside the temple. Do not measure it, because it has been given over to the nations, and they will trample the holy city for 42 months.

units.label: The two witnesses empowered to prophesy
units.note: olive trees and lampstands before the Lord

verses.text: And I will empower my two {{martys|witnesses}}, and they will prophesy for 1,260 days, clothed in sackcloth."
These witnesses are the two olive trees and the two lampstands that stand before the Lord of the earth.
If anyone wants to harm them, fire proceeds from their mouths and devours their enemies. In this way, anyone who wants to harm them must be killed.

These witnesses have power to shut the sky so that no rain will fall during the days of their prophecy, and power to turn the waters into blood and to strike the earth with every kind of plague as often as they wish.

units.label: Their death and public disgrace
units.note: the beast from the Abyss makes war on them

verses.text: When the two witnesses have finished their testimony, the beast that comes up from the {{abyssos|Abyss}} will wage war with them, and will overpower and kill them.
Their bodies will lie in the street of the great city, figuratively called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was also crucified.
For three and a half days all peoples and tribes and tongues and nations will view their bodies and will not permit them to be laid in a tomb.
And those who dwell on the earth will gloat over them, and will celebrate and send one another gifts, because these two prophets had tormented them.
But after the three and a half days, the breath of life from God entered the two witnesses, and they stood on their feet, and great fear fell upon those who saw them.
And the witnesses heard a loud voice from heaven saying, "Come up here." And they went up to heaven in a cloud as their enemies watched them.
And in that hour there was a great earthquake, and a tenth of the city collapsed. Seven thousand were killed in the quake, and the rest were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven.
The second woe has passed. Behold, the third woe is coming shortly.

units.label: The seventh trumpet: the kingdom has come

verses.text: Then the seventh angel sounded his trumpet, and loud voices called out in heaven: "The {{basileia|kingdom}} of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ, and He will reign forever and ever."
And the twenty-four elders who sit on their thrones before God fell on their faces and {{proskyneo|worshiped}} God,
saying: "We give thanks to You, O Lord God Almighty, the One who is and who was, because You have taken Your great power and have begun to reign.

The nations were enraged, and Your wrath has come. The time has come to judge the dead and to reward Your servants the prophets, as well as the saints and those who fear Your name, both small and great, and to destroy those who destroy the earth."

Then the temple of God in heaven was opened, and the ark of His covenant appeared in His temple. And there were flashes of lightning, and rumblings, and peals of thunder, and an earthquake, and a great hailstorm.

naos.gloss: The inner sanctuary or temple proper, the holy dwelling place of God, as distinct from the surrounding outer courts. John is told to measure this sanctuary and its worshipers, marking off God's true, protected people even while the outer courtyard is left unmeasured and handed over to trampling by the nations.

martys.gloss: A witness, one who testifies to what is true, often at the cost of suffering; the word gives us the English martyr, since faithful testimony repeatedly led to death. The two witnesses embody this pattern exactly, empowered to speak for God and killed for it, then publicly vindicated.

abyssos.gloss: The Abyss, the bottomless pit, a place of imprisonment for hostile spiritual powers. The beast that kills the two witnesses rises from this Abyss, showing that their opposition is not merely political but has its source in the deep, chaotic realm under God's judgment.

proskyneo.gloss: To worship, literally to bow down or prostrate oneself before someone in reverence. At the sound of the seventh trumpet the twenty-four elders fall on their faces and worship God, the fitting response of heaven's representatives to the announcement that His kingdom has fully come.

basileia.gloss: Kingdom, kingship, royal rule. The trumpet's declaration that the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ marks the theological center of the whole book, the point toward which every judgment and every act of witness has been moving.

basic.context: John is handed a measuring rod and told to measure God's true temple and its worshipers, but to leave out the courtyard, which is given over to the nations to trample for a set time. Then God empowers two witnesses to prophesy in sackcloth for the same length of time, with power to shut the sky and strike the earth with plagues, like Elijah and Moses. A beast from the Abyss eventually kills them, and their enemies celebrate publicly and refuse them burial, until after three and a half days God raises them and takes them up to heaven in full view of their enemies, followed by an earthquake. Then the seventh trumpet sounds, and heaven declares that the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of the Lord and His Christ, who will reign forever.
basic.hermeneutics: This chapter names hard, real experiences, God's people trampled, faithful witnesses killed and mocked, yet it ends in triumph, not defeat. Readers disagree over whether the two witnesses are two individual end-time prophets or a symbol of the whole church's costly testimony, and over how literally to take the numbers 42 months and 1,260 days, but nearly everyone agrees on the shape of the story: apparent defeat, public vindication, and the declared arrival of God's kingdom.
basic.originalLanguages: The naos, the inner sanctuary, and its worshipers are measured and kept safe, while the outer court is left to the nations. God's two martys, witnesses, prophesy at great cost, echoing the very word that gives us martyr. Their killer rises from the abyssos, the Abyss, showing a source deeper than mere human hostility. When the kingdom is announced, the elders proskyneo, worship, falling on their faces, because the basileia, the kingdom, of the world has become the kingdom of the Lord and His Christ.
basic.typology: The two witnesses deliberately echo Moses, who turned water to blood, and Elijah, who shut up the sky, and they also recall Zechariah's two olive trees and two lampstands feeding oil to sustain the light of witness. Their death in the street of the very city where their Lord was crucified, and their resurrection after three and a half days, retells the pattern of Christ's own death and rising, now lived out in His witnessing church.
basic.christ: The witnesses are killed in the city 'where their Lord was also crucified,' tying their suffering directly to His. Their resurrection after three and a half days and their being taken up to heaven in a cloud mirror Christ's own death, resurrection, and ascension, showing that those who bear costly testimony to Him share both His sufferings and His vindication. The chapter's climax, that the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of the Lord and of His Christ, names Jesus as the one to whom universal, everlasting reign now belongs.
basic.god: God measures and marks off His true worshipers even while permitting a season of trampling and apparent defeat. He empowers His witnesses, allows their death, and then, at exactly the right moment, breathes life back into them before a watching world. He is the Lord God Almighty who was and is and is to come, whose great power and reign, though sometimes seemingly delayed, arrives decisively and is publicly announced to all creation.
basic.crossReferences: Zechariah 4 pictures two olive trees supplying oil to the lampstand, an image reused for the two witnesses. 1 Kings 17 and Exodus 7 supply the miracles of shutting the sky and turning water to blood, tied to Elijah and Moses. And Daniel 7:14 anticipates the everlasting, universal dominion that the seventh trumpet here announces has arrived.
basic.oneStory: The people of God are measured and known even while the world tramples what looks unprotected, and His witnesses testify at the cost of their lives, only to be publicly vindicated exactly as their Lord was. This chapter is a small, vivid preview of the whole Bible's ending: suffering and apparent defeat give way, at God's appointed hour, to the open, joyful announcement that the kingdom of this world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ, forever.

context.literary:
Chapter 11 has two halves joined by the third woe that is promised and never separately described. Verses 1 to 14 finish the interlude begun in chapter 10, and verses 15 to 19 sound the seventh trumpet. The first half is itself built in three movements. A temple is measured, verses 1 and 2. Two witnesses testify, die, and are raised, verses 3 to 13. Then comes a closing notice, 'The second woe has passed,' verse 14. The time markers bind the whole together: the trampling lasts 42 months, verse 2, and the witnesses prophesy 1,260 days, verse 3, which is the same stretch counted two ways.

The scene of the witnesses moves in a pattern the reader will meet again: testimony, opposition by the beast, apparent defeat, public gloating, vindication, and a fearful response. The beast of verse 7 is the first time the word appears in Revelation, so the narrator introduces the antagonist of chapter 13 here, from the Abyss, before the dragon has been explained in chapter 12.

The seventh trumpet is surprising. The earlier six brought catastrophes on earth, but the seventh brings a hymn. Heaven speaks in the past tense, as if the reign were already here. The chapter then ends with the opening of the heavenly temple and the sight of the ark, verse 19, a pairing with the measuring of the earthly temple in verse 1. It begins with the sanctuary measured and ends with the sanctuary opened.
context.historical:
The measuring in verse 1 draws on the experience of a people whose temple had been destroyed once already. Ezekiel was shown a man with a measuring rod in a vision of a restored temple, Ezekiel 40:3, and Zechariah saw a man with a measuring line surveying Jerusalem, Zechariah 2:1 to 5. By the time John wrote, probably in the last decades of the first century, the Herodian temple in Jerusalem had been burned by Rome in AD 70, so the temple measured here cannot be that building if it was already gone, and whether John writes before or after that date is one of the points readers dispute. The picture of a temple that is protected while an outer court is trampled meant that God's presence among His people is safe even when their visible place is overrun. In Luke 21:24 Jesus Himself said Jerusalem would be trampled by the Gentiles.

The numbers 42 months, 1,260 days, and 'a time, times, and half a time' all describe three and a half years. This is the length of the drought in Elijah's day, according to Luke 4:25 and James 5:17, and the period of Daniel's suffering of the holy ones, Daniel 7:25.

The Jewish requirement that a matter be settled on the testimony of two or three witnesses, Deuteronomy 19:15, explains why the witnesses are two. Sackcloth, the rough cloth of mourning and repentance, was the dress of prophets who called for a turn back to God, as in Jonah 3:5.
context.canonical:
Chapter 11 is a mosaic of Old Testament scenes. The two olive trees and two lampstands come from Zechariah 4, where the lampstand and two olive trees stand for the anointed ones who serve the Lord of all the earth and are empowered by the Spirit, not by might, Zechariah 4:6, 14. The lampstands also recall chapter 1, where Jesus told John that the lampstands were the churches, Revelation 1:20. The powers granted to the witnesses are those of Elijah, who shut up the sky, 1 Kings 17:1, and called down fire, 2 Kings 1:10, and of Moses, who turned water to blood, Exodus 7:17 to 20. Fire from the prophet's mouth recalls Jeremiah 5:14, where God makes His words a fire in the prophet's mouth.

The rising of the witnesses echoes Ezekiel 37:10, where breath entered the dry bones and they stood on their feet. The 'Come up here' of verse 12 repeats the call of Revelation 4:1.

The seventh trumpet draws on Psalm 2, where the nations rage and God sets His king on Zion, Psalm 2:1 to 6, and on Daniel 7:13 to 14 and 7:27, where the kingdom is given to the Son of Man and to the holy ones. In the New Testament, Jesus is the faithful witness, Revelation 1:5, and His people are told that those who hold the testimony of Jesus are His witnesses, Acts 1:8. The temple opened in verse 19 recalls Hebrews 9:11 to 12 and 9:24, where Christ enters the heavenly sanctuary.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
John wrote to people who were being told, by every force around them, that the church would be crushed and forgotten. The chapter gives them the other half of the truth. The outer court is trampled, but the sanctuary and its worshipers are measured and kept. The witnesses die, but they are not silenced for good. Whatever the numbers mean precisely, the first hearers were meant to take comfort that their suffering has a limit set by God, and that it does not cancel their witness but completes it.

He also meant to correct an easy idea about success. The witnesses finish their testimony before the beast can touch them, verse 7, which means no enemy can end the mission early. Their apparent defeat comes only after the work is done. The first readers were asked to see their faithfulness as the very thing God would vindicate, not the thing that proved God had failed.

Finally, the closing hymn tells them where history is going. The kingdom of the world is passing to the Lord and His Christ, and heaven speaks as though it were done. A congregation under pressure to bow to Caesar was being told whose reign is real. The point was not to give a map of the last days but to make hearers brave enough to stay faithful where their witness would cost them.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes what happens to God's witnesses; it does not command believers to expect a precise scene. The fire from the mouth, the shut sky, the plagues, and the three and a half days of exposure are part of a vision, and Scripture nowhere tells ordinary Christians to call down fire or plagues. When James and John asked to call fire on a Samaritan village, Jesus rebuked them, Luke 9:54 to 55.

What does carry forward is the pattern of faithful testimony. God's witnesses speak His word, expect resistance, and rest in His promise of vindication. The celebration of the earth-dwellers is a warning against assuming that the world's applause means God's approval, and a comfort that the world's gloating over a fallen church is short. The chapter also gives a pattern for worship: when the kingdom is declared, the elders fall on their faces. Believers can apply the chapter not by trying to date its events but by bearing witness, trusting God for the outcome, and giving Him the glory in the face of both trampling and triumph.

debates.question: Who are the two witnesses?

views.label: Two individual end-time prophets
views.case: Their miracles closely match Elijah, who shut the sky, and Moses, who turned water to blood, and Jewish tradition expected such figures to return before the end; on this view they are two specific, individual persons raised up in the last days to confront a hostile world with undeniable, personal testimony.

views.label: A symbol of the church's corporate testimony
views.case: The number two recalls the biblical requirement that testimony be established by two witnesses, and the two olive trees and lampstands echo Zechariah's whole covenant community empowered by the Spirit to shine and testify; on this view the witnesses picture the church throughout the age, prophesying, suffering, and being vindicated together.

debates.bearing: Whether two individuals or a corporate symbol, the passage calls God's people to costly, Spirit-empowered testimony that ends not in defeat but in resurrection and open vindication before a watching world.

debates.question: How should the 42 months, 1,260 days, and the timing of this whole scene be understood, across the major interpretive schools?

views.label: Preterist
views.case: The trampling of the holy city and the death of the witnesses are tied to the actual siege and fall of Jerusalem around AD 70, a real, bounded period of Roman conquest and Jewish suffering that the first readers were living through or anticipating.

views.label: Historicist
views.case: The 1,260 days represent a long symbolic era within church history, often identified with centuries of suppressed or persecuted true testimony before a period of revival and vindication for God's faithful witnesses.

views.label: Futurist
views.case: The scene depicts a still-future tribulation period of exactly three and a half years, during which two specific prophets will testify, be killed, and be publicly and visibly raised before the final judgment.

views.label: Idealist
views.case: The numbers symbolize a limited, God-appointed season of suffering and testimony recurring throughout the church age, a pattern true in every generation rather than a chronology tied to one historical moment.

debates.bearing: All four traditions agree that whatever the length or timing, the period of trampling and testimony is bounded by God's sovereign appointment, and it ends, without exception, in vindication and the open arrival of God's kingdom.

study.originalLanguages:
The word for the measuring in verse 1 is a reed, kalamos, 'like a staff,' and the command is metreo, to measure. The verb carries the idea of marking something for protection and ownership, not only of surveying, as in Zechariah 2:1 to 5, where the measured city is surrounded by God as a wall of fire. The command in verse 2 about the courtyard is more forceful than 'exclude.' The Greek verb is ekballo, 'to cast out,' used of throwing something outside. The courtyard is left outside the measuring, and what is left outside is exposed.

The witnesses are martyres, and in the New Testament the word means someone who gives testimony, in court or in public, before it ever means someone who dies for it. The later sense, martyr, grew out of what often happened to such witnesses. In verse 7 the beast 'makes war with them and overcomes them,' a phrase that echoes Daniel 7:21, where the horn 'was waging war against the saints and prevailing against them.' The beast conquers for a time, but the vision calls the believers overcomers because of what follows.

The verb for the entry of life in verse 11 is eiserchomai, 'entered,' with pneuma zoes, 'breath of life.' It is nearly the same description as Ezekiel 37:10, where the breath entered the bones and they stood on their feet. The word for the earthquake that kills 'seven thousand' in verse 13 is literally 'names of men,' seven thousand. The number echoes 1 Kings 19:18, where God preserved seven thousand who had not bowed to Baal. Here the same number falls in judgment.

In verse 15 the Greek says the kingdom has 'become' the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ, using egeneto in the aorist, a past tense that treats the outcome as accomplished. The verb that follows, 'He will reign,' is singular: one reign belonging to both the Lord and His Christ. In verse 17 God is 'the One who is and who was,' without the usual 'and who is to come' as in Revelation 1:8, since the BSB footnote notes that this longer form is in the Textus Receptus. Many readers see significance in the shorter form: He who was coming has come. Finally, verse 18 contains a wordplay in the Greek: God will diaphtheiro, 'destroy,' those who diaphtheironas, 'destroy,' the earth. The destroyers are destroyed by the same verb.

typology.type: Moses and Elijah, the prophets of power
typology.fulfillment: The witnesses repeat the two signs most tied to Israel's founding and renewal: water turned to blood under Moses, Exodus 7:17 to 20, and the sky shut under Elijah, 1 Kings 17:1. Moses and Elijah also appeared with Jesus on the mountain, Luke 9:30. The correspondence shows the church's witness standing in the line of the Law and the Prophets. In Christ the pattern is completed: He is the prophet like Moses, Deuteronomy 18:15 and Acts 3:22, and He is greater than Elijah, since the powers shown in His ministry were not borrowed. The type falls short because the church's power is the Spirit's and its weapon is testimony, not plagues.

typology.type: The two olive trees and the lampstands, Zechariah 4
typology.fulfillment: In Zechariah the lampstand fed by two olive trees pictured the anointed servants through whom God would finish the temple by His Spirit, Zechariah 4:6, 14. John applies that scene to the church's witnesses and adds that the lampstands are the churches, Revelation 1:20. The correspondence is of a light that needs a source it does not make. In Christ the Spirit is poured out without measure, John 3:34, and believers share it, so their light is His. The type falls short because Zerubbabel and Joshua served one temple and one people, while the lampstands of Revelation are scattered through every nation.

typology.type: Death, three and a half days, and rising
typology.fulfillment: The witnesses are killed in the city where their Lord was crucified, left unburied, then raised and taken up while enemies watch. The sequence is the pattern of Jesus' own death and resurrection, followed by the ascension in a cloud, Acts 1:9. It shows that the disciple's path follows the Master's, Romans 8:17. The escalation in Christ is that He rose on the third day by His own authority and secured the resurrection of all who are His, 1 Corinthians 15:20. The type falls short because the witnesses' rising is a vindication of faithful servants, while Christ's resurrection is the ground of every other.

typology.type: The ark of the covenant seen in heaven, verse 19
typology.fulfillment: The ark was the place of the mercy seat where God met His people, Exodus 25:22, and the glimpse of it in the opened heavenly temple tells of covenant faithfulness at the very hour of judgment. It points to Christ, who entered the greater and more perfect tabernacle with His own blood, Hebrews 9:11 to 12, and to the throne of grace, Hebrews 4:16. The type falls short because the earthly ark was hidden from all but the high priest once a year, whereas the heavenly one is open.

study.christ:
The chapter reaches Christ in several ways, and the closest link is the pattern of the witnesses' fate. They die in 'the great city, where their Lord was also crucified,' verse 8. The words are plain: the witnesses are servants of a Lord who was killed, left, and raised. Their story is shaped as a retelling of His in the lives of His people. His warning, 'No servant is greater than his master,' John 15:20, becomes a scene. His promise, 'Because I live, you also will live,' John 14:19, becomes a standing on their feet.

It reaches Christ also by title. Verse 15 calls Him 'His Christ,' the anointed one, and so this is the Messiah of Psalm 2, whom the nations rage against and to whom God has given the nations as an inheritance, Psalm 2:2 and 2:8. The seventh trumpet is the Father's announcement of what the cross and resurrection achieved. The kingdom does not come in the abstract; it becomes 'the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ.' The Son of Man to whom Daniel saw dominion given, Daniel 7:13 to 14, has received it.

It reaches Christ by contrast with the trampled court. The Lord who said 'Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up again,' John 2:19, spoke of the temple of His body, John 2:21. The sanctuary that is measured and kept is where His presence is, and Paul says that the church is a temple of the living God, 2 Corinthians 6:16, and Peter that believers are a spiritual house, 1 Peter 2:5. So the measuring of the temple has Christ at its centre, the one in whom the dwelling of God with man is secure.

It reaches Christ also by the open heavenly temple. Hebrews describes Christ as the high priest who passed through the heavens and entered the true sanctuary, Hebrews 4:14 and 9:24. The ark that appears in verse 19, the seat of mercy, is the place of His atonement, and its appearance in the midst of lightning and hail says that God's mercy and judgment are not separate.

The danger to avoid is making each detail a Christ-code. The two witnesses are not Christ, and the 1,260 days are not a coded timeline of His life. The link is the New Testament's own: the faithful witness who died and lives, Revelation 1:5, and the kingdom given to Him, which this chapter announces.
study.god:
The seventh trumpet gives a vivid picture of God's sovereignty. The elders praise Him as the One 'who is and who was,' and they say He has 'taken Your great power and has begun to reign.' The word begun matters: His reign is not new in being but new in open display. God has always been king, Psalm 93:1 and 103:19, but now He has taken up the power against all rivals. Rebellion has been real, and chapter 11 does not downplay it, but God is never merely a spectator.

He is the God who gives His servants a work and protects it until it is done. The witnesses are 'empowered' by Him, and nothing can touch them until they have finished their testimony. The same God who permits the beast to overcome them also raises them. The tension between permitting and protecting is real, and the chapter holds it without resolving it. God lets His witnesses suffer, and God vindicates them. His sovereignty is wider than the protection of His servants from pain, and it is certain.

He is just, and He is also merciful. The seventh trumpet announces wrath on the raging nations, but it also announces rewards for prophets, saints, and 'those who fear Your name, both small and great.' Judgment is not blind: the God who destroys those who destroy the earth is the God who cares about the earth He made. After the earthquake, the survivors 'gave glory to the God of heaven,' verse 13. Whether this is true repentance or only terrified acknowledgement is debated, since in Revelation 9:20 to 21 and 16:9 people refuse to repent and give Him glory, but the text at least lets the door stand open.

He is the God who keeps covenant. The ark appears in His temple, and the one who sits above the ark is the God of promise. Lightning and thunder come from the same place as the mercy seat. For worship the chapter teaches the posture of the elders: falling on their faces, giving thanks, naming God by what He has done. It teaches believers to sing the end of the story while still standing in the street of the great city, since the one who has begun to reign cannot be dethroned.

crossReferences.note: The vision of the lampstand and two olive trees, explained as the anointed ones who stand by the Lord of the whole earth. The same phrase is used of the witnesses in verse 4. The key line, 'Not by might nor by power, but by My Spirit,' Zechariah 4:6, names the source of the witnesses' strength.

Elijah announces that there will be neither dew nor rain except at his word. James 5:17 says the drought lasted three and a half years, the same length as the witnesses' ministry. The shut sky of Revelation 11:6 is a deliberate echo of this prophet's power.

Moses strikes the Nile and the water becomes blood. The witnesses' power to turn waters to blood in verse 6 recalls this first great plague against Egypt's gods. The mention of 'Egypt' in verse 8 shows that the city is treated like the oppressor of God's people.

The breath entered the dry bones, and they came to life and stood on their feet. The language of Revelation 11:11 is nearly the same. The scene presents the witnesses' resurrection as God's own life-giving act, the answer to the vision of a dead people.

The horn waged war against the saints and prevailed against them. The beast's war with the witnesses in verse 7 repeats the wording. The Daniel passage then goes on to the judgment and to the kingdom given to the saints, Daniel 7:22, which the seventh trumpet announces.

One like a son of man receives dominion, glory, and an everlasting kingdom. The heavenly voices of Revelation 11:15 announce that the kingdom of the world has become that very kingdom, given to the Lord and His Christ, and that He will reign forever.

The nations rage and plot against the LORD and His Anointed, and God speaks to them in His anger. Revelation 11:18 draws on this, as the BSB footnote notes, with the rage of the nations answered by God's wrath. The Anointed One is installed on Zion in spite of them.

A matter is to be established on the testimony of two or three witnesses. This is why the witnesses are two. Their testimony is legally sufficient, and a world that rejects it has been given a complete hearing.

Jesus says that Jerusalem will be trampled by the Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled. The trampling of the holy city for 42 months in verse 2 uses the same image, and both passages set a limit on the trampling.

Christ came as high priest of the good things to come and entered the greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made with hands, by His own blood. The opening of the heavenly temple in Revelation 11:19 shows the sanctuary where this service is done.

study.oneStory:
From the first chapters of Genesis the Bible keeps one conflict in view: who will rule the world God made. The serpent claimed it in the garden, the nations claimed it at Babel, and Pharaoh claimed it over Israel. The prophets answered that God would take back what is His. Psalm 2 and Daniel 7 are the two great statements: the nations will rage, and then the kingdom will be given to the Anointed One and the saints.

Revelation 11 is where that answer is announced as accomplished. The verse that everything has been waiting for is verse 15: the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ. The long history of tyranny, from Egypt to Babylon to Rome, is shown to be on a short leash, measured in months and days.

Before that moment, though, the chapter shows what the interval is like. God's people live as a trampled court, and God's witnesses are killed in the street. The pattern is the same as it was for Joseph, for Moses, for the prophets, and for Jesus: faithful testimony, rejection, and a vindication that comes from God alone. The church lives in the time between the ascension and the return by repeating the story of its Lord in miniature.

The chapter also looks forward to the end of the book. The judgment of the dead and reward of the servants, verse 18, will be seen in Revelation 20:11 to 15. The open temple and ark point toward the day when the temple is no longer needed because the Lord God and the Lamb are its temple, Revelation 21:22. The kingdom that is announced here is the one in which 'He will wipe away every tear,' Revelation 21:4, and the God who has begun to reign will reign in a restored creation forever.

quiz.q: What is John told to do with the courtyard outside the temple?

options.text: Exclude it from the measuring, because it has been given over to the nations to trample for 42 months.
options.note: Revelation 11:2 gives this exact instruction.

options.text: Measure it more carefully than the temple itself.
options.note: The opposite is commanded; the courtyard is specifically excluded from measuring.

options.text: Destroy it immediately.
options.note: John is told to measure or not measure, not to destroy anything himself.

options.text: Give it to the twenty-four elders.
options.note: It is given over to the trampling nations, not to the elders.

quiz.q: What imagery from the Old Testament describes the two witnesses?

options.text: The two olive trees and two lampstands that stand before the Lord of the earth.
options.note: Revelation 11:4 draws this directly from Zechariah's vision.

options.text: The two tablets of the Ten Commandments.
options.note: The text specifically names olive trees and lampstands, not tablets.

options.text: The two cherubim over the ark of the covenant.
options.note: Cherubim are not the image used here; olive trees and lampstands are.

options.text: The two pillars of Solomon's temple.
options.note: The passage names olive trees and lampstands from Zechariah's vision, not the temple pillars.

quiz.q: What happens to the two witnesses after they finish their testimony?

options.text: The beast from the Abyss wages war on them, overpowers them, and kills them.
options.note: Revelation 11:7 states this directly.

options.text: They are welcomed as heroes by the nations.
options.note: The opposite occurs; their enemies gloat over their deaths rather than honoring them.

options.text: They retire peacefully and are never heard from again.
options.note: They are killed publicly, and then dramatically raised and taken to heaven, not left in quiet retirement.

options.text: They are given a proper burial by the nations.
options.note: The text says the opposite, their enemies refuse to let their bodies be laid in a tomb.

quiz.q: What happens three and a half days after the witnesses are killed?

options.text: The breath of life from God enters them, they stand up, and they are taken up to heaven in a cloud before their enemies.
options.note: Revelation 11:11-12 describes this resurrection and ascension.

options.text: Their bodies simply disappear without explanation.
options.note: The text specifically describes God reviving them and their visible ascension, not a mere disappearance.

options.text: The nations finally bury them with honor.
options.note: Instead, God raises them publicly rather than the nations changing their treatment of the bodies.

options.text: They are replaced by two new witnesses.
options.note: The same two witnesses are raised and ascend; they are not replaced.

quiz.q: What is announced when the seventh trumpet sounds?

options.text: That the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ, who will reign forever and ever.
options.note: Revelation 11:15 records this declaration exactly.

options.text: That the trumpet judgments are cancelled.
options.note: Far from cancelling judgment, the trumpet announces the arrival of God's reign and the time to judge and to reward.

options.text: That the beast from the Abyss has won.
options.note: The declaration is the opposite, the victory and reign belong to the Lord and His Christ.

options.text: That the temple in heaven will remain closed.
options.note: Revelation 11:19 says the temple of God in heaven was opened, not kept closed.

questions: God measured and marked off His true worshipers even while the outer courtyard was given over to trampling. Where do you need to trust that God knows and protects what looks unguarded in your own life?

The two witnesses testified faithfully even though it cost them their lives, and their enemies celebrated their deaths. What would faithful testimony cost you this week, and are you willing to pay it?
The witnesses were publicly humiliated for three and a half days before God raised and vindicated them. How does their story help you wait through seasons when faithfulness seems to end in defeat?
The seventh trumpet declares that the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of the Lord and His Christ. How would living as though that is already true change your priorities this week?
The elders responded to God's reign with worship and thanksgiving. What is one specific way you can respond to God's sovereign rule with worship today rather than anxiety?

translationNotes.note: 42 months, 11:3's 1,260 days, and 12:14's 'a time, and times, and half a time' are parallel ways of naming the same symbolic span, roughly three and a half years, half of the number seven, picturing a limited, broken period of trial rather than necessarily a precise, literal calendar length.

'Figuratively' translates a Greek term meaning spiritually or symbolically, signaling that Sodom and Egypt are not literal place names for the city but theological labels for its moral corruption and opposition to God.
'Three and a half days' is a short, symbolic mirror of the longer three and a half years already mentioned, underlining that even a brief period of apparent triumph for evil is firmly bounded by God.
'Loud voices' rather than a single voice suggests a great heavenly chorus, matching the scale of the announcement that the kingdom of the world has become the Lord's.
